1:
Gill dates it to Sivan, answering to part of May and June. Clarke reports that the same day has been read three ways, all with respectable arguments behind them: the same day of the month as that on which they left Egypt, or a day of the same number as the month, or the first day of the month. He prefers the last and gives the arithmetic — forty-five days from the departure to the first of the third month, Moses going up on the second, three days granted the people to purify themselves, which brings us to the forty-ninth; and on the next, the fiftieth from the passover, the glory appeared. Henry and Wesley both make that fifty the point, and Henry adds the calculation that went wrong: in Egypt they had spoken of a three days' journey into the wilderness to the place of their sacrifice, and it proved almost a two months' journey — so often are we out in the reckoning of times, and things prove longer in the doing than we expected. Clarke notes that the hill has two peaks, Horeb being probably the older name, and Sinai coming from the seneh, the bush — or rather the thicket of bushes — in which the Angel appeared.

Calvin asks what the apparatus of the chapter is for, and answers that it was to render the people attentive and teachable before the laws were promulgated. God had already delivered the rule of a just and pious life; by writing the Law on tables and adding its exposition he ratified it by a solemn rite, that the recognition of it might flourish in future times. The covenant with Abraham was eternal and inviolable, but it had grown into disregard from the lapse of time and the carelessness of mankind, and needed renewing — engraved on stone and written in a book, that the grace conferred on Abraham's race should never sink into oblivion. Yet the Law has a peculiar property: it covenants conditionally. Calvin distinguishes the general doctrine Moses delivered, which everywhere holds forth the hope of pardon, from the special office imposed upon him, to demand perfect righteousness and promise a reward on no condition but that they fulfil whatever was enjoined. Which is why Paul says the Law was added because of transgressions, sets it against the promise given to Abraham, and calls it the ministration of death.

The preparation by terror follows. Since men's minds are partly swollen with pride and partly stupefied by indifference, Calvin says, they must be either humbled or awakened before they will receive divine teaching, and none is prepared to obey God till he is bowed down and subdued by fear. Henry takes the charter from the other end and finds grace throughout. The maker and first mover of the covenant is God himself: nothing was said or done by this unthinking people towards it, no petition put up for God's favour, but the charter was granted purely out of his own good-will. Free grace anticipates us with the blessings of goodness; we love him and covenant with him because he first loved us and covenanted with us, and God being the Alpha must be the Omega. Henry finds the same tenderness in the eagle. Other birds carry their young in their talons, but the eagle upon her wings, so that archers who shoot flying cannot hurt the young unless they first shoot through the old one — which is what the pillar of cloud and fire did at the Red Sea, interposing itself between Israel and its pursuers. Even Egypt, that iron furnace, was the nest in which these young ones were hatched, and when they grew to some maturity they were carried out of it; their way, so paved and so guarded, was glorious, but their end much more so — I brought you unto myself.
2:
Where exactly they camped is disputed on the ground itself. Ellicott places Rephidim in the Wady Feiran and the march from it at eighteen or twenty-five miles, according to the valley taken; the wilderness of Sinai he identifies with Er Rahah, a plain two miles long by half a mile wide, enclosed between precipitous ranges of granite with the prodigious block of Ras Sufsafeh at its end, nearly flat, and better supplied with water than any spot in the peninsula. He notes what matters for what follows: the Ras Sufsafeh is visible from every part of the plain. Keil denies the identification outright. The desert of Sinai is not er Rahah, which lies north of Horeb, but the desert in front of the mountain; and he argues from usage: the mountain is called Sinai throughout Israel's stay and the encampment always the desert of Sinai, never of Horeb, though the same spot is once called Mount Horeb and Deuteronomy as a rule says simply Horeb.

Calvin reads the ascent as habit rather than event. Moses sought retirement, as he was wont, to take counsel of God; going up to God means no more than that he went out of the camp, that far from the multitude he might inquire in secrecy what was God's pleasure — not choosing a lofty position to be nearer God, as the superstitious do, but withdrawing from disturbance to engage all his senses in learning. Ellicott notices that he was called while still on his way, and spares a sentence for it: God meets us half-way when we arise and go to him. Then the eagle, on which they do not agree at all. Ellicott takes the received account, that when its young are first fledged the eagle assists their flight by flying beneath them, so that they may settle upon its wings. Clarke reports Bruce's contention that the word does not mean the eagle at all but the rachama, a bird the Arabs name for its kind disposition and its care in carrying its young upon its back. Calvin will have none of the mechanism: that eagles alone bear their young upon their wings he calls a foolish and truly Rabbinical gloss, the figure meaning rather that eagles lift their young to high places and accustom them to look at the sun, so that the people, carried as if above the clouds, had surmounted every obstacle.

The treasure is a technical word, and each handles it. Keil says segullah means not property in general but valuable property, what is laid by or put aside, a treasure of silver and gold. Ellicott derives it from a root meaning to earn or acquire, a possession the owner got by his own exertions, God viewing Israel as made his own by the long series of mighty works done for their deliverance; the word stands here for the first time and afterwards becomes a standing epithet for the nation. Calvin prefers a root meaning to mark with the owner's seal, a possession on which the owner has stamped his mark. Wesley guards the metaphor from the obvious misreading: not that God was enriched by them as a man is by his treasure, but that he valued them as a man does his treasure, keeping them under special care as a thing kept under lock and key. On the clause that follows, for all the earth is mine, Calvin and Ellicott pull opposite ways. Calvin takes the particle adversatively, so that God exalts his grace by setting this one nation against the whole world; Ellicott takes it as a check on exactly that, since in claiming a peculiar right in Israel God does not mean to separate himself from the other nations or give them up to their own devices — Israel is the favoured son, but the rest are all of them children of the Most High.
6:
Gill reads the phrase against their recent history: instead of servitude they are erected into a kingdom, a free state governed by its own laws, and those of God's making, with God himself more immediately their king. He passes on Jarchi's alternative, a kingdom of princes, illustrated from the Roman senate, of which the ambassador of Pyrrhus said he had seen at Rome as many kings as senators. All the Targums, he notes, render it kings and priests. Ellicott divides the two words and gives each its content: kings as lords over themselves, equals one to another, owing allegiance to God only; priests as entitled to draw near to God in prayer without an intermediary, to bring him their offerings and pay him their vows. Calvin agrees that both honours are meant, and prefers this reading to the passive one that makes God their king, because it is the reading Peter takes up — and when the Jews who had refused Christ still gloried in the title, Peter claimed the honour for the members of Christ only, since Christ appeared invested with kingdom and priesthood in order to confer both upon his members.

What kind of holiness the second phrase names is where they part. Ellicott is explicit that it is not the duty of personal but the privilege of official holiness that is intended: each Israelite was to be as near to God, as fully entitled to approach him, as the priests of other nations either were or thought themselves; personal holiness was the natural outcome of that official holiness, but is not what the words say. Calvin says the same and then joins the two back together — the nation is called holy not with reference to piety or personal holiness but as set apart from others by special privilege, yet upon this kind of sanctification the other depends, since those exalted by God's favour should cultivate holiness and so on their part sanctify God. Clarke will not make the distinction at all. They should be a holy nation, saved from their sins, righteous in their conduct, holy in their hearts, every external rite being not only a significant ceremony but a means of conveying light and life, grace and peace to everyone who conscientiously used it — an institution, he adds, which could not receive its perfection except under the Gospel.

Ellicott explains the machinery of the answer, the elders being the usual channel between Moses and the people, reporting his words to them and theirs to him; and he flags the translation, since before their faces is a curious literalism for what in Moses' time was a mere preposition meaning before. Wesley finds more in the phrase: Moses not only explained what God had given him in charge but put it to their choice whether they would accept these promises on these terms, and his laying it to their faces speaks his laying it to their consciences. The answer came back without a dissenting voice, and Ellicott catches its temper — no hesitation, no diversity of opinion, no self-distrust, and in the glow and warmth of their feelings the difficulty of perfect obedience did not occur to them. Calvin knows what follows and refuses either to excuse it or to call it a lie. Soon after they relapsed and did not keep their promise in the smallest degree; yet we may believe they spoke without dissembling, and that without any intention of deceiving God they were carried away by a headlong zeal and deceived themselves. Moses does not reproach them with having lied; by recording how ready they were to obey, he deprives them hereafter of all pretence of ignorance. Let us learn to sift ourselves, Calvin ends, lest we rashly promise more than we are able to perform.
9:
The cloud is a veil, and the commentators say why one was needed. Ellicott puts it as a paradox: though God is light — nay, because he is light — clouds and darkness are round about him, and he must be closely veiled when he draws near to men, since otherwise they could not endure for a moment the brightness of his presence. Henry gives the veil a second office: the thick cloud was to prohibit curious enquiries into things secret and to command an awful adoration of what was revealed, so that though they saw no manner of similitude they should see enough to convince them that God was among them of a truth. Clarke reads the cloud against the next paragraph, where the mount is altogether on a smoke, and marks the contrast with the pillar's usual appearance, generally clear and luminous.

The stated purpose is Moses' credit, and Calvin builds a rule of authority on it. By a manifest symbol of his glory God would make it evident that the Law proceeded not from Moses, who merely delivered faithfully what he had received from heaven; and there is no other mode of proving a doctrine than the assurance that it comes from God alone. That levels every teacher: if the mightiest of the prophets obtained credit on no other ground than that he bore God's commands, how foolish and impudent it is in teachers who sink far beneath him to aim at a higher point. Nor was the credit meant to last a short time, for the call of some is temporary, but God so appeared to Moses as to consecrate the truth of his doctrine in all ages. Ellicott asks whether it worked, and answers that on the whole it did: God has remained to the Israelites, for more than three millennia, an awful power, real, personal, tremendous, and the Law has remained the guide of their life — though the living Moses was often resisted and contemned, the dead Moses has been reverenced and obeyed from his death to the present time.

Sanctification comes next, and Ellicott divides it. The real preparation for approach to God is inward, but no external command can secure that, so Moses was instructed to issue directions for outward purification, and it was left to the people's spiritual insight to perceive that such purity symbolised and required the internal kind as its counterpart. Henry treats the washing exactly so: not that God regards our clothes, but while they were washing them he would have them think of washing their souls by repentance — it becomes us to appear in clean clothes when we wait upon great men, and clean hearts are required in our attendance on the great God, who sees them as plainly as men see our clothes. Calvin adds the reason for insisting at all, that God would not cast pearls before swine, and turns it on the reader: it is the just reward of profanation that so many readers or hearers profit nothing by heavenly doctrine, because they rush in without fear or reverence, as to some ridiculous stage play. He then raises the objection himself. If faith purifies the heart, and understanding goes before faith since faith comes by hearing, is not the order inverted when the people are sanctified before they hear the Law? His reply is that faith alone truly purifies, but this does not prevent the fear of God going before to prepare a place for the word, a pious desire of learning being properly the commencement of faith. On the washings Clarke and Ellicott notice the same parallel and draw it oppositely: Clarke holds that the heathens borrowed their purifications before sacrifice from these institutions, while Ellicott records only that the same idea prevailed in Egypt, Greece and Rome.
11:
Ellicott insists the barrier was artificial, dismissing Stanley's suggestion that a line of natural mounds near the base represents it, though allowing that Moses' fence may have followed the natural line. He explains why one was needed: travellers observe how abruptly the precipice of Ras Sufsafeh rises from the plain, so that in many places a man may stand on level ground and still touch the mountain. He names the impulse it was against: unless it had been forbidden there might have seemed no reason why pious Israelites should not climb the height to draw near to God in prayer — a praiseworthy feeling, the one that breathes in the words nearer, my God, to thee, but the nation was not fit for close approach. Calvin turns the same point into a rule for readers. By this symbol the people were admonished to restrain their inquisitiveness, since God by the teaching of his Law enlightens only those who are as little children; all would have wished to come like Moses to familiar converse with God, and are commanded instead to stand within the boundaries. What was enjoined then extends to us: in reading and hearing we should not overpass the limits God assigns, but content with the doctrine he delivers, let alone what he would have concealed, and not be offended that he speaks from afar. Wesley draws the comparison that follows: noticing the distance at which worshippers were then kept should make us value the more our boldness to enter into the holiest.

The next clause is mistranslated, and all four of them say so: there shall not a hand touch it should be him, the transgressor and not the mountain. Ellicott explains the point of it: to stop the man and seize him another person would have to cross the bounds himself and repeat the very act forbidden, so he was to be stoned or transfixed with arrows from within the barrier. Gill reads it so too: no man should follow him to lay hold on him, but dispatch him at once. Calvin thinks both of those miss it. Moses' object was to make such men detestable: he commanded them killed at a distance, as if whoever touched them even with a finger would contract pollution, so that they were avoided as accursed lest they infect others by their contagion. Clarke agrees: the offender was to be treated as an unclean and accursed thing, not to be touched for fear of conveying defilement.

Two questions remain, and they divide on both. Ellicott holds that the permission to come up when the trumpet sounds long is not general: the word they is emphatic and refers to privileged persons, Moses and Aaron, not to the people at all, so that what is forbidden in one verse is allowed in the next but not to the same men. Calvin reads it as an assurance to the whole nation, given lest the people should think themselves rejected and, offended by the ignominy of the repulse, abandon their desire for the Law. The other question is the abstinence. Ellicott sets it among the customs of the ancient world, where it was the general sentiment that a ceremonial uncleanness attached even to the chastest connection — a view held by the Greek and Roman writers, by the Levitical law, and by the Indian, Persian and Mahometan codes. Clarke proposes instead that the words have been misread: the verse forbids approaching a mountain burning with fire, and the phrase rendered come not at your wives may rather mean come not near unto the fire, ishshah being esh transposed, for which he offers parallels of alternate forms. Gill closes with Aben Ezra's guess that perhaps not a man slept that night, so as to hear the voice of the Lord in the morning, as the high priest used to keep awake before the day of atonement.
16:
Henry stages the whole thing as a sermon, and Wesley reproduces his account almost word for word. The preacher was God himself, who descended in fire; the pulpit, or throne rather, was the mountain, hung with a thick cloud, covered with smoke, and made to quake greatly, so that Sinai itself, rough and rocky as it was, melted from before the Lord God of Israel. The congregation was called together by a trumpet exceeding loud and waxing louder, and the introductions to the service were the thunders and lightnings. Henry puts their purpose as two questions: were the people asleep? the thunders would waken them; were they looking another way? the lightnings would turn their faces towards him that spoke. Thunder is the voice of God and lightning the fire of God, engaging the two senses by which we take in most of what we know. Clarke can imagine the storm but not the trumpet — of the thunders, and of the deep, dark, dismal cloud from which they proceeded, we can form a tolerable apprehension, but of that loud, long-sounding blast we can scarcely form a conjecture, unless it were something like the trumpet of the angel who swears that there shall be time no longer.

Getting them there was not simple. Gill supposes that a people already panicking at the sound came out of the camp with difficulty, and that nothing short of Moses going at their head could have prevailed on them to leave it. Ellicott fixes the ground: an open space must have lain between the camp and the bounds, and into this Moses led them, as near to God as was permitted, in the plain directly in front of Ras Sufsafeh and almost under it. Henry finds the sentence worth stopping on. He that had led them out of the bondage of Egypt now led them to receive the law from God's mouth — public persons are indeed public blessings when they lay out themselves to promote the public worship of God, and Moses at the head of an assembly worshipping God was as truly great as Moses at the head of an army in the field.

Clarke reads the staging as evidence. Some particular proof of God's being and power was necessary if a people so deplorably prone to idolatry were to be kept from it, and the proof was given in a form that left no room for suspecting Moses of a cheat. He makes much of the three days' notice: it gave them time to sanctify themselves, and it gave any sceptic among them full opportunity to take every precaution against being imposed on, so that the previous warning strongly serves the cause of revelation. Calvin sees a double purpose in the terror and will not let either half go. Partly it was to set the presence of God before their eyes, that his majesty might urge the beholders to obedience and vindicate his doctrine from contempt; partly it was to express the nature of the Law, which in itself produces nothing but mere terror, being given to cite slumbering consciences to the judgment-seat, that through fear of eternal death they might flee for refuge to God's mercy. And yet the prodigies were not meant to drive the people away. They are commanded to go and meet God, presenting themselves with minds ready unto obedience, which could not be unless they heard in the Law something besides precepts and threatenings; God's covenant, Calvin says, was no less lovely than alarming.
18:
Gill is careful to say what the smoke was not: not natural, as with volcanoes, but so dense that nothing else could be seen — and he reads it as an emblem of the darkness of the legal dispensation, full of obscure types and figures, dark shadows and smoky sacrifices, against which the clear day of the Gospel stands. Ellicott takes the Hebrew as smoked, all of it, and rejects the softening some prefer, that dense clouds merely had the appearance of smoke: if the mountain burned with fire, as Deuteronomy asserts, the smoke was real. He reads the quaking as literally as the smoke, since the expression suits an earthquake better than the vibration that very violent thunder sometimes produces.

Calvin values the accompaniments as corroboration. Had Moses been the only spectator of God's glory the credit of his testimony would be lighter; but having reported the commandments which God spoke with his own lips in the hearing of the people, he adds that the lightnings shone openly, the mountain smoked, the trumpets sounded and the thunder rolled — so that by these conspicuous and illustrious signs the law was ratified before the whole people, from the greatest to the least. Then the people's own confession follows, when, overwhelmed with alarm, they beg that God speak no more; and after that they could no longer despise the voice of the man whom they had themselves asked for as mediator. They were terrified, Calvin insists, not that they might be stupefied with astonishment but that they might be humbled and submit — and it is a peculiar privilege that the majesty of God, before whom heaven and earth tremble, does not destroy his children but only proves and searches them.

Gill hears the trumpet change character at this point: not one continued even tone as before, but going and strengthening itself exceedingly, rising to a pitch so vehement as scarce to be borne. On the descent he enters the usual caution, that the coming down is in visible tokens of presence and power, since otherwise God is the incomprehensible Jehovah who fills heaven and earth and can be contained in neither. Ellicott locates it exactly, on the summit of the Ras Sufsafeh and not the Jebel Musa, which is out of sight from the plain. Clarke sets out the whole arrangement in tiers — the glory upon the top, with Moses permitted to approach near it; Aaron and the seventy elders allowed some way up; the people only at the base; and the traffic running down the same steps, Moses receiving the statutes from God's mouth, Aaron and the elders from Moses, and the people acting on what they received. Nothing, he says, could be imagined more glorious, terrible and majestic; but it was chiefly calculated to impress deep reverence and sacred awe, and he who attempts to worship God uninfluenced by these has a proper sense neither of the divine majesty nor of the sinfulness of sin.
21:
The prohibition has been given already, and Calvin asks why it is given again. Because once was not enough, and God knew he had to do with the rebellious, for whose subjugation a sorer dread of punishment was necessary; so he insists with greater vehemence and repeats the charge with threatenings. Since we are no better than they, Calvin adds, let us not be surprised if God often spurs us on by many exhortations and redoubles his threats, for otherwise forgetfulness of all he has once enjoined would creep over us. The passage also confirms for him that curiosity is greatly displeasing to God — not because God would have anything concealed which it were profitable to know, but because inquiry ought to be sober, and this is the legitimate limit of knowledge: humbly to learn at God's mouth what he voluntarily teaches, not to advance with too anxious longings, but to follow him as he leads. Ellicott glosses the danger literally, as forcing a way through the barrier, and thinks the perishing threatened may be less the execution of the earlier sentence than a heaven-sent stroke like the one that fell on the men of Beth-shemesh.

The priests named here are a difficulty, since Aaron has not yet been consecrated, and all four handle it. Ellicott states the objection and dismisses it: this has been called an anachronism, but the Israelites, like every other ancient race, must have had priests long before this, appointed on one principle or another, and it is a reasonable conjecture that the heads of families had hitherto exercised sacerdotal functions. Clarke argues it from the narrative — Moses had asked Pharaoh for liberty to go into the wilderness and sacrifice, a request that would have been absurd had there been neither sacrifices nor priests among the people — and adds a reason for their needing to sanctify themselves now, that no sacrifices had been offered for a considerable time, so that the priests themselves were reckoned in a state of impurity. Gill canvasses the three candidates, the firstborn, the sons of Aaron who were priests potentially though not yet actually, and the heads of families, and settles on the last, ruling out princes on the ground that the description will not fit them. Calvin agrees, allowing that priests were chosen from the firstborn but doubting that out of so immense a multitude there was a special priest for every house; since no heathen nation was then without priests, there was no less method among the chosen people.

Moses then argues back, and Calvin watches him lose. Persuaded the people would be obedient, he replies that the decree already pronounced was sufficient and a repetition supererogatory, putting himself forward as their surety — honestly, and in accordance with the rule of charity, yet, as God's reply shows, deceived, because he judged others by his own feelings. What Calvin admires is that he executes the order without hesitation, preferring God's command to his own settled opinion, and so teaching by example that whatever imaginations come into our minds must be brought under this yoke, that God's authority alone may have the pre-eminence. Ellicott finds the flaw in the argument exactly: Moses means they cannot come up unwittingly, and does not contemplate a deliberate trespass — which was the thing God knew to be contemplated. Clarke allows both readings of the impossibility, that they dared not with instant death before their eyes, or that the barrier made it physically impossible; and on the last word he notes that sanctify is here used in its proper literal sense, of separating a place from all profane and common uses and devoting it to sacred ones.
24:
God does not take the objection. Ellicott marks the moment with a phrase from the epistle — he with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning, overrules Moses and persists; the warning is required, and it is to be given; Moses, submissive as usual, yields and goes down and speaks to the people. And Ellicott records the outcome, which is easy to miss: no attempt to break through the barrier was made. Gill reads the urgency in the wording, that the Lord knew better than Moses did, so that it was high time for him to be gone and the matter required haste, the people standing under a great temptation to indulge their curiosity at the peril of their lives.

Clarke supplies the reason God overruled a man who was, on the face of it, right about his own people. God knew that they were heedless, criminally curious and stupidly obstinate, and therefore his mercy saw it right to give them line upon line, that they might not transgress to their own destruction. What looks like excessive repetition is, on that reading, the same care that set the bounds in the first place. And from the whole solemn and awful manner in which the Law was introduced, Clarke draws the conclusion the chapter has been building toward: we may behold it as the ministration of terror and death, appearing rather to exclude men from God than to bring them nigh.

From which it follows, he says, that an approach to God would have been for ever impossible had not infinite mercy found out the Gospel scheme of salvation; and he sets the two mountains side by side as the epistle does — not the mount that might be touched and that burned with fire, nor blackness and darkness and tempest and the sound of a trumpet and the voice of words, which they that heard entreated should not be spoken to them any more, but Mount Sion, and the city of the living God, and Jesus the Mediator of the new covenant. Clarke then turns and addresses the reader directly, asking whether he is still afar off, under the condemning power of that fiery law, and answering that though a man has deeply sinned and God is just, he is also the justifier of him that believeth — obey his voice indeed and keep his covenant, and thou shalt be a king and a priest unto God and the Lamb, which returns the chapter to the promise it opened with. Gill closes on the last verse more quietly, with Moses charging the people to keep their distance behind the line he had drawn; and he passes on what the Targums add to the charge, that they were to come and receive the ten words.
